title: same_origin ignores the scheme, so a plaintext http:// page on the same host passes the CSRF origin check of a TLS deployment
description: Every cookie-authenticated UI mutation ultimately relies on same_origin() (api.py:108-110), which compares only urlsplit(Origin).netloc with the Host header and never the scheme. Verified in-sandbox: http://H, http://H:8765, and http://agentbox.example.com are all accepted against the matching Host, while sibling same-site, wrong port, and null are rejected. In a TLS deployment a page served as plaintext http://H (forgeable by an active network attacker; no Strict-Transport-Security is set anywhere in agentbox/, deploy/ or images/, and Caddy's reverse_proxy adds none) has a different web origin from https://H but passes this check. On a browser WITHOUT schemeful same-site, http://H and https://H count as same-site, so a SameSite=Strict Secure cookie (desktop.py:53) would be attached to the auto-submitted cross-scheme POST and agentbox would accept it. Id-free actions: POST /logout (ends the server session and hands desktop takeover back to the agent) and POST /ui/sandboxes (creates a sandbox with an attacker-supplied source_dir). Approve/deny additionally needs the 48-bit apr_ approval id (approvals.py:51, token_hex(6)), so a blind attacker is limited to the id-free actions. DECISIVE CAVEAT from parent-live evidence (agents/parent-live/artifacts/l3/l4.out, script l4.cjs): on Chromium 141 the cross-scheme POST had same_origin accept its Origin but the Secure SameSite=Strict cookie was NOT attached (schemeful same-site), so the session-ending and create attacks fail there; the only effect was the unconditional r.delete_cookie on the logout response clearing the browser cookie client-side (forced browser logout) WITHOUT ending the server session. Firefox and WebKit were not tested. The finding therefore stands only on browsers without schemeful same-site; the exploitable browser population and the HSTS/active-network-attacker deployment facts remain open.
claimed_root_cause: api.py:108-110: same_origin() accepts when urlsplit(origin).netloc == headers['host'] with no scheme comparison, so the cross-origin defence degrades to the browser treating http/https of one host as cross-site; nothing in source emits Strict-Transport-Security (deploy/Caddyfile, agentbox/ and images/ set none), so an active network attacker can serve http://H.

trace.scope: decide (POST /ui/approvals/{aid}/{decision}); also create web.py:160, logout web.py:128
trace.description: Cookie-authenticated, form-encodable POST routes reachable by a cross-origin auto-submitted form; verified these are the state-changing UI mutations gated only by the cookie session plus same_origin.
Resolves the cookie session via box.desktop.session_scope(cookie) (api.py:119), then same_origin(request.headers) at api.py:122 is the only origin binding for the cookie principal.
Returns True when urlsplit(origin).netloc equals Host; independently confirmed http://H matches Host H and missing Origin is allowed, so scheme is never compared.
box.decide(aid, approve, actor='human', session=p.session) executes with the victim's session; peer id-free sinks are create_sandbox at web.py:164 and end_ui_session at web.py:132.

evidence.description: Netloc-only comparison with no scheme check. Reproduced in-sandbox (agents/v01/artifacts/v01_same_origin.out): accepts http://H vs Host H, http://H:8765 vs H:8765, http://agentbox.example.com vs that host, and missing Origin; rejects sibling same-site, wrong port, and null.
set_cookie issues the session cookie HttpOnly, samesite='strict', secure=secure; under non-schemeful same-site http://H and https://H are same-site, so the Strict cookie is not separated by scheme.
s.secure_cookie = s.secure_cookie or tls or behind: the Secure attribute is set for direct-TLS and behind-TLS-proxy deployments, which is the deployment class this finding targets.
reverse_proxy site block emits no Strict-Transport-Security; grep over agentbox/, deploy/ and images/ found no HSTS anywhere, so the browser is not forced to upgrade http://H to https.
logout's only guard is the scheme-blind same_origin (web.py:130); end_ui_session (web.py:132) ends the server session and hands takeover leases back to the agent when the cookie is present.

Parent-live (not a verifier reproduction) real Chromium 141, script l4.cjs: cross-scheme POST http://127.0.0.1 -> https://127.0.0.1/logout had same_origin accept the http Origin (netloc==Host) but the Secure SameSite=Strict cookie was NOT attached (schemeful same-site); server session not ended, only the delete_cookie forced a client-side logout. Resolves the Chromium 141 case as non-exploitable; Firefox/WebKit untested.

blockers: Browser behaviour (decisive): whether any operator browser lacks schemeful same-site and so attaches a SameSite=Strict Secure cookie to a cross-scheme form POST from http://H to https://H. Only Chromium 141 was tested (cookie NOT attached, l4.out); Firefox and WebKit current behaviour and the legacy-version cut-offs are untested and cannot be determined from source.
Deployment: whether the production host sends HSTS or is preloaded (none in source), and whether an active on-path network attacker who can serve plaintext http://H is in scope.

validation_plan.local: Isolated loopback browser lab: map H to 127.0.0.1, run a dummy agentbox with --tls-cert (self-signed, lab-trusted) on 443 and a plaintext http://H listener on 80 auto-submitting forms to https://H/logout and /ui/sandboxes. The parent already ran this on Chromium 141 and the Secure SameSite=Strict cookie was not attached (agents/parent-live/artifacts/l3/l4.out). Remaining local steps: repeat with current Firefox and WebKit, and with any browser/version or policy that disables schemeful same-site: log in to https://H, open http://H, and check whether agentbox_session is sent and the POST is accepted (303) rather than 403, and whether the server session is actually ended. Regression check on the fix: same_origin({'origin':'http://h','host':'h'}) must return False once the full scheme+netloc origin is compared.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner confirms whether the production hostname sends HSTS (or is on the preload list) and which browser engines and versions operators actually use; if all are schemeful-same-site browsers and/or HSTS is present, the finding is not reachable. No live probing of deployed endpoints.

title: The UI and CLI audit timelines stop at the 5000th row, so an agent can push its later actions out of the human's view
description: The sandbox page's audit fragment (GET /ui/audit, re-polled every 3 s) and `agentbox audit` both fetch rows with AuditLog.list(limit=5000) and no after_id. AuditLog.list is `WHERE id > ? [AND sandbox_id = ?] ORDER BY id LIMIT ?`, so it returns the OLDEST 5000 matching rows, and nothing is ever pruned. Once a sandbox (sandbox page, `agentbox audit --sandbox`) or the whole system (default `agentbox audit`) holds more than 5000 rows, the UI shows the last 400 of the oldest window (ids 4601-5000, total capped at 5000) and the CLI prints rows 1-5000. Every later row (tool_request/tool_result, snapshot, human_takeover/handback, gui_processes_stopped, gui_changes) is never shown, while the UI footer keeps saying it shows the most recent 400 of 5000. The UI window is per sandbox; the default CLI view is system-wide, so one sandbox's volume also hides other sandboxes' later events from it. A prompt-injected agent that holds only its own sandbox's agent token can reach the threshold without any approval: one approval_forbidden row per refused POST /approvals/{any id} (no Docker, no rate limit; needs raw API access with the token), or three rows per allowed tool call such as list_dir or exec of an allowlisted read-only command (about 1,670 calls through the ordinary MCP tools). Correction to the hunter's example: `exec true` is not an approval-free path, because default_policy.yaml lists true/false unquoted (line 27) and PyYAML parses them as booleans, so that call returns 202 and needs approval; `exec ls`, `exec echo` and list_dir are allowed. Long-lived ordinary sandboxes reach the same threshold without any attacker. The rows stay in the database, GET /audit?after_id=... returns them, verify passes and the approval queue is unaffected; only the two views humans actually use stop updating.
root_cause: AuditLog.list (audit.py:190-197) can only return the oldest `limit` rows after `after_id` (ORDER BY id ascending). Both human-facing consumers call it with limit=5000 and no after_id and then treat the result as the newest window: web.py audit_frag takes rows[-400:] and total=len(rows), and cli.py cmd_audit prints the whole list. Beyond 5000 rows the 'tail' is the tail of the oldest 5000, never the newest rows, and total is capped at 5000. Neither the UI nor the CLI has a paging control and the audit table is never pruned, so the freeze is permanent for that sandbox or system.
intended_behavior: The sandbox page timeline (footer: only the most recent N shown, total M) and `agentbox audit` show the newest audit events with the real total, or page through all rows. The volume of rows an agent can create must not hide its later events from the human's oversight views, in particular the gui_changes and gui_processes_stopped records that the README (line 198) names as the way the human sees changes made through the ungated GUI path.

Ordinary allowed tool calls (POST /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/{tool}: list_dir, read_file, exec of an allowlisted command, GUI tools) also add rows, three each via service.py:297, 305 and 359.

No request-rate limit (none in the app or in deploy/), no tool_pool slot, no Docker call and no row cap; tool_concurrency only bounds simultaneous tool calls.

'WHERE id > ? [AND sandbox_id = ?] ORDER BY id LIMIT ?' returns the oldest rows first. Rows are never deleted (UPDATE/DELETE triggers), so once the limit is exceeded newer rows are only reachable by paging with after_id.
rows = box.audit.list(sandbox_id=sandbox_id, limit=5000): the oldest 5000 rows of that sandbox, no after_id. This is the fragment sandbox.html:19 re-requests every 3 s.

evidence.description: ' ORDER BY id LIMIT ?' is ascending, so any limit keeps the oldest rows; the same query serves the unpaged UI/CLI callers and the after_id paging API.
The UI takes the tail of the oldest-5000 window and reports total as len(rows), which cannot exceed 5000.
Footer '최근 {{ rows|length }}개만 표시 (전체 {{ total }}개)' (most recent N shown, total M) is false beyond 5000 rows; the harness printed '최근 400개만 표시 (전체 5000개)' with 5012 rows in the database.

cmd_audit requests /audit with limit=5000 and no after_id and prints everything it gets; there is no paging flag, and without --sandbox the query is system-wide. Real cmd_audit printed ids 1..5000 only.

GET /audit returns list(..., after_id=after_id, limit=min(limit, 5000)) with a default limit of 500: an unpaged call returns the oldest 500 rows (measured: newest id 500 of 5012); only after_id paging reaches newer rows, and neither the UI nor the CLI pages.
The sandbox page polls /ui/audit?sandbox_id=... on load, every 3 s and on audit-changed: this is the live oversight view, and its only other audit-related control is the verify button.
Every tool call appends tool_request here, policy_decision at line 305 and (when allowed and executed) tool_result at line 359: measured exactly 3 rows each for exec ls and list_dir.
default: allow, so list_dir, read_file, write_file and the GUI tools have no rule and need no approval; the read-only-exec allowlist (lines 25-27) allows ls, echo, cat and similar.

true and false are unquoted, so yaml.safe_load yields booleans and the allowlist holds 'True'/'False', not 'true'/'false'; measured: exec true returns 202 (approval requested), so the hunter's `exec true` example is wrong (the root cause is unaffected).

gui_changes (and gui_processes_stopped at line 225) are written only to the audit log and rendered only by web.py describe (line 62) and cli.py (line 280), so the two timelines are the only human-facing surface for them.
Documents the timeline as where the human sees the 'deleted: ...' list and the snapshot id for GUI-path changes; the README's known limitations do not mention a 5000-row cap.
The suite asserts that the /ui/audit page shows '삭제됨: old-report.md', confirming the timeline is the designed surface for gui_changes; no test brings a sandbox anywhere near the 5000-row limit.

Rows can be created through the ordinary tool endpoints and MCP tools (list_dir, read_file, exec of an allowlisted command: 3 rows per call) or, with raw API access, by refused POST /approvals/{id} (1 row per call).

The human relies on the sandbox page timeline or `agentbox audit` output rather than paging GET /audit with after_id; the UI and CLI have no paging control.

Step 0-1: with the sandbox's agent token send POST /approvals/apr_probe (403) and three probe tool calls (exec ls and list_dir are allowed and add 3 rows each; exec true returns 202 and needs approval), then 4,990 more refused POST /approvals/apr_N so the table holds exactly 5000 rows for sb_v02. Inspect the template context and the unrelated sandbox's page.

Step 5-7: call the real cli.cmd_audit (default, --sandbox sb_v02, --sandbox sb_other) through a shim that injects the human token; GET /audit (default and after_id=5000) and /audit/verify; exercise the proposed remediation (newest-N plus COUNT(*) query, CLI after_id paging loop) on the same database.
execution.observed_result: With exactly 5000 rows the sandbox page showed ids 4601..5000 and the newest shown id equalled the newest in the database (boundary control). After 12 more rows (ids 5001-5012: exec and click tool_request/policy_decision/tool_result, snapshot 5006, gui_processes_stopped 5008, gui_changes 5009 for sb_v02; 5010-5012 for sb_other) the poll for sb_v02 returned status 200, template _audit.html, 400 rows, ids 4601..5000 (all approval_forbidden), total 5000, footer '최근 400개만 표시 (전체 5000개)', with no id above 5000, no gui_changes, no gui_processes_stopped and no AFTER_FLOOD_MARKER; the unrelated sb_other page still showed its own rows 5010-5012. Real cmd_audit printed 5000 lines, ids 1..5000, and none of the markers for both the default and --sandbox sb_v02; --sandbox sb_other printed ids 5010-5012. An unpaged GET /audit returned the oldest 500 rows (newest id 500). GET /audit?after_id=5000 returned ids 5001-5012 and /audit/verify returned ok=True over 5012 rows, so nothing is lost, only not shown. Proposed fix on the same database: the newest-400 plus COUNT(*) query returned ids 4610..5009 with total 5009 including gui_changes, and the CLI paging loop returned all 5012 rows. A second run gave identical numbers. Not executed: real Jinja2 rendering (unavailable in sbx), Docker-backed SandboxManager.

remediation.strategy: Make the human views read the newest rows and report the real total. Add AuditLog.recent(sandbox_id, limit) = SELECT COUNT(*) plus 'ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?' under the same lock, use it in web.audit_frag (newest first, matching the existing template), and make `agentbox audit` page /audit with after_id until an empty page (optionally add a --tail N flag or a newest-first /audit option so large logs are not transferred in full). Replace the same oldest-first pattern in web.verify_frag (web.py:270, limit=100000) with a point lookup of the broken id. Optionally add an index on audit(sandbox_id, id) for the filtered COUNT and reverse scans (CREATE INDEX does not conflict with the append-only triggers). Regression tests: append 5100 rows for one sandbox, assert GET /ui/audit renders id 5100 with total 5100 and that cmd_audit's fetch includes id 5100; assert the same for a sandbox filter when another sandbox holds most of the rows.

code_changes.fixed_code:
def recent(self, sandbox_id: str | None = None, limit: int = 400) -> tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], int]:
        """Newest `limit` rows (newest first) and the real row count for the same filter."""
        where, args = (" WHERE sandbox_id = ?", [sandbox_id]) if sandbox_id else ("", [])
        with self._lock:
            total = self.conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM audit" + where, args).fetchone()[0]
            rows = self.conn.execute(
                "SELECT id, ts, sandbox_id, actor, event, tool, payload, prev_hash, hash FROM audit" + where
                + " ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?", args + [limit]).fetchall()
        return [
            {"id": r[0], "ts": r[1], "sandbox_id": r[2], "actor": r[3], "event": r[4], "tool": r[5],
             "payload": json.loads(r[6]), "prev_hash": r[7], "hash": r[8]}
            for r in rows
        ], total

likelihood.reason: No approval and no Docker work are needed: the rows come from the agent's own requests. In the harness 4,991 refused POST /approvals/{id} calls (one row each; needs raw API access with the agent token) took about 15 s in-process, and each allowed list_dir/read_file/exec of an allowlisted command adds exactly 3 rows (about 1,670 calls through the ordinary MCP tools, no raw API access needed). tool_concurrency (4 simultaneous) only slows this; there is no request-rate limit or row cap. Long-lived ordinary sandboxes cross 5000 rows without any attacker. It needs a human who relies on the timeline rather than paging /audit, and the frozen window stays visible (400 rows, constant total), so an attentive operator could notice that it stopped advancing.

impact.reason: Both human timelines (the sandbox page polled every 3 s, and `agentbox audit`) stop advancing while the UI footer claims to show the most recent rows, so later tool_request/tool_result, snapshot, takeover/handback, gui_processes_stopped and gui_changes rows are not shown. The README names the timeline as the way the human sees gui_changes, the compensating control for the ungated GUI path, so the lowest-trust principal can silence that control for itself at will. The default CLI is system-wide, so one sandbox's volume also hides other sandboxes' later events from `agentbox audit` without --sandbox; the per-sandbox UI window of an unrelated sandbox was not affected (checked). Bounded: no row is lost or altered (GET /audit?after_id= returns them, verify passes), the approval queue, snapshots, stray-process kill and tool gating are unaffected, and there is no disclosure or privilege gain.

confidence.reason: Reproduced twice with identical numbers through the real api.build() app: agent-token HTTP requests created the rows, the real service.py code wrote gui_processes_stopped and gui_changes, and the real web.py audit_frag route and real cli.cmd_audit ran. Only Docker (SandboxManager) and Jinja2 rendering were stubbed, and the footer text came from the real _audit.html line. The boundary control (exactly 5000 rows shows the newest row), the unrelated-sandbox control and the paging/verify checks support the causal reading, and the ordering, the limit, the missing paging and the absence of any documented cap are direct from source. The hunters' artifacts (h-audit, h-wild) agree.

title: agentbox agent prints sandbox file contents, file names and model text raw to the operator terminal, bypassing cli._safe
description: cli._safe exists so agent-determined strings never reach the terminal as raw control or bidi characters, and the approval and audit views use it. cmd_agent's log() prints model text ('say'), tool-call arguments ('call') and the first 6 lines of each tool result ('result') without it. read_file returns /workspace file bytes as-is, and list_dir returns raw `ls -la` output. Docker exec_run has no tty, so GNU ls quotes nothing and control characters in file names come through. A file the operator hands to the agent (source_dir, upload, or written into /workspace) can therefore put ESC sequences on the operator's terminal when the LLM loop reads it. Reproduced with the real cli.main(['agent', ...]), the real ToolClient and OpenAIChat over loopback HTTP: 7 raw ESC bytes, a full OSC 52 sequence, one raw U+009B, and a file name with ESC[2K from real non-tty ls. In a VT emulator (pyte), the content erased the '→ read_file(...)' line and the start of the file, then showed a forged '[사용자] ok, nothing else to do' line. exec results go through json.dumps(ensure_ascii=False), which escapes ESC as \u001b but keeps 8-bit C1 such as U+009B, and whether that acts depends on the emulator. Impact is limited to spoofing the transcript that `agentbox agent` displays. The approval prompt (`agentbox approve`, rendered with _safe) and the audit log are not affected, and no authority is gained. Clipboard writes (OSC 52) and C1 handling were emitted but not observed in a real emulator and are not claimed.
root_cause: cli.py:353-361 cmd_agent.log prints 'say', 'call' and 'result' strings without cli._safe, and agent.py:116-126 ToolClient.call_text passes read_file content and list_dir listings through verbatim (other results via json.dumps(ensure_ascii=False), which keeps C1 controls).
intended_behavior: As the cli._safe docstring (cli.py:37-39) and _UNSAFE (cli.py:34) say, strings determined by the agent, the sandbox or the model are shown with C0/DEL/C1 and bidi controls made visible (newlines preserved for multi-line results), the same way _show_approval and cmd_audit render them.

trace.description: Bytes of a /workspace file (controlled by whoever supplied or wrote it, lower trust than the operator) are decoded and returned as 'content' with no filtering; list_dir at 548-552 returns raw non-tty `ls -la` output the same way.
Under the default policy, read_file and list_dir are allowed without approval. The full result goes back in the 200 body unchanged; only the audit log gets a summary (_summary).
read_file content (and list_dir listing at 121) becomes the tool text verbatim; other tools use json.dumps(ensure_ascii=False), which escapes C0 but not C1.
log('result', text) passes the tool text to the CLI logger; model text goes through log('say', ...) at 256.
print() writes the first 6 result lines raw to the operator's stdout; the 'say' branch at 355 and the 'call' branch at 357 also print without _safe.

evidence.description: _safe docstring: agent-determined strings are not printed to the terminal as-is; control characters are shown as \x1b.
_show_approval applies _safe to every line of the approval card (also 203 and 246 in audit), so cmd_agent.log is the inconsistent exception.
list_dir runs `ls -la` through exec_run without a tty. In this verifier's run, GNU coreutils 9.4 ls printed a dummy file name containing ESC[2K raw.
The default is 'allow' and no rule covers read_file or list_dir, so no approval stands between the file content and the terminal.
json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False) turns ESC into \u001b (observed) but leaves U+009B raw (observed).

Verifier v03b's reproduction (real cli.main/ToolClient/OpenAIChat over loopback stubs, in sbx): ESC count 7, OSC 52 present, ESC file name from ls raw, pyte screen loses the read_file call line and 'Quarterly report' and shows the forged [사용자] line.

The parent's run of h-wild's harness (fake LLM/ToolClient) rendered in pyte: two prior lines erased, forged '[agent] Summary' line, window title set to 'owned-title'. Its base script (/scratch/l6_base.py) was not retained, so this only corroborates.

title: Exposed-serve runc guard checks only the literal runtime name 'runc', so the Docker-registered alias io.containerd.runc.v2 bypasses it and suppresses the dev-only warnings
description: Candidate: cmd_serve refuses to expose a control plane whose sandbox runtime is runc unless --allow-runc / AGENTBOX_ALLOW_RUNC is set, but runtime_problem (cli.py:84) and the warning sites (cli.py:116 and 140, api.py:443, base.html:44, desktop.py:342) compare against the literal 'runc'. If the operator pins AGENTBOX_RUNTIME=io.containerd.runc.v2, which Docker lists and _detect_runtime accepts, an exposed plane starts without --allow-runc and the red dev-only badge and healthz dev_only flag disappear. Verification: the mechanism reproduces exactly as described in the sbx sandbox (auto and runc are refused when exposed; the alias is selected, runtime_problem returns None, serve starts silently, healthz dev_only is false, no desktop badge) and every cited line is accurate. What does not hold is the security classification: the selector is operator-controlled, the same operator can already opt in with --allow-runc, and no trust boundary is crossed (see reason).
claimed_root_cause: runtime_problem and the dev-only warning sites decide on the runtime name string 'runc' instead of its isolation class, while _detect_runtime accepts any name Docker lists, so runc-class names such as io.containerd.runc.v2 (and crun or nvidia where an operator registers them) are treated as strong isolation.

trace.description: AGENTBOX_RUNTIME is read from the launcher's process environment into Settings.runtime. This is operator-controlled, not a lower-trust entrypoint: no agent, UI-session, desktop-link or API principal can set it (no os.environ write in the package, no runtime field in CreateSandbox, compose does not forward it).

An explicit pin is accepted whenever Docker's info()['Runtimes'] lists it (io.containerd.runc.v2 is listed on this host); the error at line 301 only enumerates available names. 'auto' (303-306) can never return the alias.

exposed is computed at line 108 (TLS, behind-proxy or non-loopback bind); runtime_problem(box.sandboxes.runtime, exposed) is consulted and serve exits only when a problem is returned and --allow-runc / AGENTBOX_ALLOW_RUNC is absent (109, 111-113).
`if runtime != "runc" or not exposed: return None` is a literal-name check, so the alias returns None (reproduced); the local warnings at cli.py:116 and 140 use the same literal.

Containers are created with runtime=self.runtime (the alias if pinned). healthz (api.py:443), base.html:44 and desktop.py:342 then omit the dev-only indicator while the runtime name itself is still printed (api.py:442, base.html:43, desktop.py:284).

evidence.description: Literal-name check that lets io.containerd.runc.v2 through when exposed (reproduced in the sandbox harness).

Documented operator opt-out (--allow-runc / AGENTBOX_ALLOW_RUNC=1) starts exposed serve on runc with a loud warning (cli.py:115); the alias reaches the identical state without the flag, so it grants nothing the operator could not already choose.
The serve banner prints the selected runtime name at startup (reproduced: 'io.containerd.runc.v2' is shown).

_RUNTIME_PREFERENCE (kata-fc, kata-qemu-firecracker, runsc, runc) is all that 'auto' can return with the fallback at 303-306; reproduced: auto resolves to runc on this host's runtime list and the guard fires.
Explicit pin accepted whenever Docker lists the name; on this host the list is io.containerd.runc.v2 and runc (architecture.md section 3).
CreateSandbox accepts only source_dir and template: there is no per-request or per-principal runtime selector (human-only endpoint).
The UI create form likewise takes only template and source_dir.
healthz dev_only is the literal comparison; line 442 still reports the runtime name (reproduced via the real function body).
Every UI page header prints the runtime name next to the isolation label.
The red dev-only badge appears only for the literal 'runc'.
Desktop page badge only for the literal 'runc' (reproduced with the real desktop.page); line 284 still prints the runtime name.
The sandbox_created audit event records the runtime name.

The compose service forwards only AGENTBOX_HOME, AGENTBOX_BEHIND_TLS_PROXY and AGENTBOX_ALLOW_RUNC; AGENTBOX_RUNTIME is not forwarded (confirmed by a static YAML parse), so the shipped deployment resolves to auto and is refused on this host.
Documents the guard for the case where no strong runtime exists and the install would fall back to runc, which is the guarded auto path.
AGENTBOX_RUNTIME is documented as an operator override pinned to runsc or runc.
The unit test encodes the intended contract: only literal runc is flagged when exposed; runsc, kata-fc and kata-qemu-firecracker pass (lines 127-130).

reason: Mechanism reproduced; security classification refuted. No lower-trust principal controls the selector and no trust boundary is crossed, which is the same ground on which run-1 rejected the desktop-ticket claim. REPRODUCED (sbx harness agents/v04/artifacts/v04_alias.py, output agents/v04/artifacts/v04_runtime_alias.out; real cli.runtime_problem and cmd_serve, real SandboxManager._detect_runtime, real desktop.page and healthz body; only Docker info() and uvicorn.run / api.build are stubbed; Docker Runtimes = [io.containerd.runc.v2, runc] per architecture.md section 3): AGENTBOX_RUNTIME unset/auto and runc resolve to runc and 'serve --host 0.0.0.0 --behind-tls-proxy' is refused; AGENTBOX_RUNTIME=io.containerd.runc.v2 is selected, runtime_problem returns None, the same serve command starts with no stderr warning, healthz dev_only is false and the desktop red badge is absent; crun, nvidia and runsc fail at startup on this host because they are not registered. All hunter line numbers and descriptions check out. WHY IT IS NOT A FINDING. (1) The first trace entry is not a lower-trust entrypoint: Settings.runtime comes only from the launcher's process environment (config.py:31). A static scan of the flat agentbox package finds no os.environ write and a single .runtime assignment (sandbox.py:293); POST /sandboxes and the UI create form take only source_dir and template (api.py:45-47, web.py:161); the compose file forwards only AGENTBOX_HOME, AGENTBOX_BEHIND_TLS_PROXY and AGENTBOX_ALLOW_RUNC (docker-compose.yml:18-25). Agent, UI-session, desktop-link and human-token principals cannot influence it, and the candidate itself states that no attacker action is involved. (2) No unauthorized action: the operator who must type the alias can already reach the identical state with --allow-runc / AGENTBOX_ALLOW_RUNC=1 (cli.py:109-115) or the bare uvicorn factory (api.py:448-450), so the bypass grants nothing beyond that documented consent; the alias is Docker's name for the containerd runc shim (runc-class, shared host kernel, as the candidate itself assumes) and the container hardening flags (sandbox.py:374-383) are unchanged. (3) Default and documented paths stay guarded: auto never selects the alias (sandbox.py:81, 303-306), README:81 describes the no-strong-runtime fallback that is guarded, README:265 documents pinning with runsc or runc, and the shipped compose never sets AGENTBOX_RUNTIME. The accident story is weak: the startup error only lists available runtimes and both listed names contain 'runc'. (4) 'Humans are told isolation is not runc' is overstated: the runtime name is printed in the serve banner (cli.py:122), every UI header (base.html:43), the desktop page (desktop.py:284), /healthz (api.py:442), create output (cli.py:139) and the sandbox_created audit event (service.py:431); only the red badge and the dev_only boolean are missing. (5) Impact is not demonstrated: harm needs a separate container-escape bug and equals the already accepted --allow-runc state, so the hunter's low/low/low rating has no lower-trust path to rest on (at most informational); crun and nvidia would pass only if an operator registers them in the Docker daemon. RETAINED AS HARDENING, NOT A FINDING: unlike bind_problem (allowlist-shaped, fails closed for unknown hosts), runtime_problem is a one-name denylist that fails open for unknown runtime names (CWE-184). Suggest one helper built on a strong-runtime allowlist (runsc*, kata*, with an override for custom-named strong runtimes) used at cli.py:84/116/140, api.py:443, base.html:44 and desktop.py:342, plus a regression test that runtime_problem('io.containerd.runc.v2', True) is not None.

title: Rotating the human token does not revoke existing full-admin browser sessions (no revoke-all; sessions persist 12 h across restart)
description: Web UI cookie sessions (scope '*') are rows in ui_sessions: sha256(cookie), a public hs_ id, created, expires = creation + 12 h, scope. Nothing ties a row to the human token that authorised it. When the owner rotates the shared admin secret (a new AGENTBOX_HUMAN_TOKEN, or deleting/regenerating data/human_token) and restarts, the old token stops working (Bearer 401; /login issues no cookie), but every '*' cookie minted under it keeps working until its fixed 12 h expiry, because DesktopControl.__init__ deletes only expired rows and session_scope checks only the cookie hash and expiry. There is no bulk revocation: no route, method or CLI command does it; logout and login/ticket redemption act only on the presented/new cookie and never end a replaced one; no API accepts the hs_ id that the audit log records. A holder of an earlier-minted agentbox_session cookie therefore keeps the full browser-UI authority after the owner has withdrawn the only credential: the same Depends(browser_human) gate admits approve/deny of agent actions, sandbox delete/restore/snapshot, file upload, outbox download, sandbox creation with an arbitrary host source_dir (only data-folder overlap is refused) and desktop takeover, and the desktop WebSocket gate accepts the cookie too. README.md documents the 12 h life and persistence across restart as a known limit but is silent on rotation and revocation.
root_cause: Session validity is independent of the credential that created it: the ui_sessions schema (desktop.py:35-37) has no token-generation or lineage column, DesktopControl.__init__ (desktop.py:91-93) prunes only expired rows, session_scope (desktop.py:133-145) checks hash and expiry only, and no code path deletes more than one session at a time (end_session, desktop.py:127-131), so only the session's own logout or its 12 h expiry ends it. The human token is read once at start-up (config.py:88, api.py:66) and used only for comparisons, so rotating it changes nothing stored in agentbox.db.
intended_behavior: A browser session is valid only while the human credential that authorised it is still current: rotating the human token (new AGENTBOX_HUMAN_TOKEN or regenerated data/human_token) invalidates every browser session and unredeemed ticket minted under the old one, while a restart with an unchanged token keeps logins (tests/test_m4_acceptance.py::test_login_survives_restart); the owner has an explicit revoke-all that needs no rotation; and a login that replaces a cookie ends the replaced server-side session. The README documents none of the rotation/revocation guarantees, so this is the security expectation for a shared-admin-secret model, not a documented promise.

trace.description: POST /login (unauthenticated network client holding the then-current token) compares the form token with human_token (compare_digest, web.py:120) and calls start_session (web.py:95-101), which calls DesktopControl.new_session() with the default scope '*'. GET /login?ticket= (web.py:109-113) and the per-sandbox ticket route (api.py:298-308) mint sessions the same way.
Inserts (sha256(cookie), public hs_ id, created, expires = now + 12 h, scope) at lines 123-124; nothing records which human token authorised the session (schema lines 35-37).

Rotation = new AGENTBOX_HUMAN_TOKEN or a deleted/regenerated data/human_token, read once at start-up (api.py:66) and used only for compare_digest checks (api.py:96, web.py:120) and log masking; nothing in agentbox.db changes.
On restart only rows with expires < now are deleted (lines 92-93); the table is dropped only for the legacy no-scope schema (lines 86-89).
With no Authorization header the cookie goes to box.desktop.session_scope (line 119); same_origin (line 122) passes when Origin is absent; returns Principal('human', session, scope) (line 124).

The only verification: SELECT by sha256(cookie) and reject if expires < now (lines 138-145). No token generation, lineage or revocation check; a cookie minted under the rotated-out token returns (public id, '*').

p=Depends(browser_human) = api.screen_human (api.py:126-132) admits the scope-'*' stale session; box.decide(...) runs with the stale session id (web.py:209). The same gate fronts every other /ui admin route, sandbox create (source_dir), delete, restore, snapshot, upload, outbox and takeover.

evidence.description: ui_sessions columns are hash, public, created, expires, scope only (PRAGMA output in agents/v05/artifacts/v05_rotation.out line 4): no token generation.

Start-up prunes only expired sessions. The only other deletions are single-hash logout (130), per-lookup expiry (143), expiry cleanup in new_session (122) and the legacy scope-less table drop (89); nothing deletes sessions in bulk and nothing extends expires (grep of agentbox/).
session_scope: SELECT by hash, reject only if expires < now.
end_session deletes exactly one hash.
Logout ends only the presented cookie (via service.end_ui_session, service.py:517-527).

start_session (POST /login and GET /login?ticket=) mints a new session without reading or ending a cookie already presented; api.py:306 does the same for per-sandbox tickets (the hunter's api.py:306 evidence covers only that route). Harness: v05_rotation.out lines 38, 41, 43, 47.
human_token is read once in build(); rotation therefore needs a restart and touches nothing in agentbox.db.
Known limitations: login sessions last 12 h and survive a restart; nothing about rotation or revocation (README.md:193 covers only expiry/deletion of one session).
test_login_survives_restart pins persistence across a restart with an unchanged token as intended; no test or code considers rotation.

Independent reproduction after rotation + restart on the same agentbox.db: old token 401 (line 12) and no cookie from /login (14); cookie minted under it gets /ui 200 (20), /ui/approvals 200 (21), /ui/sandboxes 200 (22); an approval decision is accepted and audit-logged under the stale session id (25-29); WS gate passed (30); 43199 s left (33); forged/no cookie controls 401 (16-18); regenerated data/human_token gives the same result (51-54).

Route inventory of the real app: the cookie principal reaches POST /ui/approvals/{aid}/{decision}, POST /ui/sandboxes, POST /ui/sandboxes/{sid}/delete, restore, snapshots, POST /sandboxes/{sid}/files, outbox, capture.png and desktop takeover/handback/state; only /logout matches session/revoke/logout (line 34) and no revoke/logout-all attribute exists (35).

Patch validation: a token-generation binding drops sessions and tickets on rotation (lines 2-3), keeps them across a restart under the same token (1, 4-5), adds revoke_all (6-7), migrates legacy databases (8-10); the repo's session/ticket/lease unit tests pass against the patched class (11).

conditions.description: Attacker holds a '*' agentbox_session cookie minted before the rotation (former operator, shared browser profile, or a login made with the since-rotated token). The old token alone is not enough after rotation (Bearer 401; /login issues no cookie).
Owner rotates the human token (new AGENTBOX_HUMAN_TOKEN, or deletes/regenerates data/human_token) and restarts against the same agentbox.db (the default; AGENTBOX_HOME/AGENTBOX_DB unchanged).
Use within the cookie's original 12 h life: the expiry is fixed at creation and no code path extends it, so a session minted just before the rotation gives the longest window.

execution.attacker_perspective: A former operator (or other holder of an earlier-minted '*' browser session cookie) who is meant to be cut off when the owner rotates the shared human token and restarts the control plane; the attacker sends ordinary browser requests with the old agentbox_session cookie, no Authorization header and no Origin header.
payloads: POST /login  form token=hum_V05_old_dummy_token_aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa -> 303, Set-Cookie agentbox_session=<cookie_old>; HttpOnly; Max-Age=43200; SameSite=strict
restart: api.build() with AGENTBOX_HUMAN_TOKEN=hum_V05_new_dummy_token_bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb on the same AGENTBOX_HOME/agentbox.db (variant: delete data/human_token and restart)
GET /sandboxes with Authorization: Bearer <old token> -> 401; POST /login with the old token -> no cookie
GET /ui, /ui/approvals, /ui/sandboxes, /ui/audit, /ui/notify with Cookie: agentbox_session=<cookie_old> (no Authorization, no Origin) -> 200
POST /ui/approvals/<pending dummy approval id>/deny with the same cookie -> 200; approval becomes denied; audit approval_decision records session=<hs_ id of cookie_old>
WS /sandboxes/sb_v05dummy/desktop/ws?mode=view with Origin http://testserver and the old cookie -> closed 1011 (past the 4401/4403 gates); no or forged cookie -> 4401
instructions: Ran agents/v05/artifacts/v05_rotation.py as 'sbx v05 /usr/bin/python3.13 -I -B /scratch/v05_rotation.py' (no network, no Docker socket, read-only target and /usr, scratch-only writes, uid 65534, empty allow-listed environment, 512 MiB, 1 CPU, 64 pids, 120 s).

Docker is replaced by a dummy client (info() -> runc) and Jinja2 (not installed in the sandbox) by a stub registered as fastapi.templating. Authorization runs in route dependencies before any render, so the stub cannot change an auth decision: forged or absent cookie -> 401 on the same routes where the stale cookie gets 200.

Part A: api.build() with AGENTBOX_HUMAN_TOKEN=OLD, POST /login, keep cookie_old, close; api.build() again on the same AGENTBOX_HOME with AGENTBOX_HUMAN_TOKEN=NEW (the restart). Probe with Bearer OLD, form login OLD, forged and no cookie (controls) and cookie_old; create a pending dummy approval for dummy sandbox sb_v05dummy and deny it with cookie_old; open the desktop WebSocket gate for the dummy sandbox id; read ui_sessions and enumerate the routes whose auth dependency accepts the cookie principal.

Part B repeats the rotation by deleting data/human_token and restarting (regenerated token). Part C posts /login, redeems a '*' ticket and a per-sandbox ticket, and logs out, each while presenting an existing cookie, then checks which sessions remain valid. Part D moves the stale row's expiry into the past to show that only the TTL ends it.

Part E (and v05_fix_check.py with desktop_fixed.py, a scratch copy of desktop.py plus the patch below; target files untouched) applies the proposed generation binding in memory and repeats the rotation; the repo's own session/ticket/lease unit tests pass against the patched class.
execution.observed_result: After rotation + restart on the same database: Bearer OLD -> 401 and POST /login with OLD -> no cookie; forged or absent cookie -> 401 (GET /ui -> 303 /login). The cookie minted under OLD gets GET /ui 200, /ui/approvals 200, /ui/sandboxes 200, /ui/audit 200, /ui/notify 200; POST /ui/approvals/<dummy>/deny -> 200 and the dummy approval became denied, with an approval_decision audit entry carrying the stale session's hs_ id; the WebSocket gate accepted the stale cookie (close 1011 on the non-existent dummy sandbox) while no or forged cookie got 4401; the row had 43199 s left. Deleting/regenerating data/human_token gave the same result (token1 Bearer 401, cookie1 -> 200 on /ui/approvals and /ui/sandboxes). The session table and DesktopControl expose no revoke/logout-all, and the only session route is /logout. Logging in, redeeming a '*' ticket or a per-sandbox ticket while presenting a cookie left the presented session valid, and logout ended only its own cookie. Only expiry (moved into the past) ended the stale session (401). With the generation-binding prototype: old cookie -> 401 after rotation, new-token login 200, restart with an unchanged token keeps the login (200). Not exercised (no Docker): approve, delete, restore, upload, source_dir sandbox creation; they share the same authorization gate.

remediation.strategy: Bind sessions and tickets to the human token that minted them and give the owner a way to revoke: store a domain-separated hash of the human token (token_gen) in a gen column of ui_sessions and ui_tickets, delete rows whose gen differs at start-up (a rotation then drops all old sessions and unredeemed tickets, while a restart with an unchanged token still keeps logins) and require gen in session_scope; add a human-only revoke-all (DesktopControl.revoke_all, a bearer-authenticated route and an 'agentbox logout-all' command) that deletes all sessions and tickets and cuts live screen connections (the 30 s session_watch re-check in api.py already hands back leases once the rows are gone); end the replaced server-side session when a login or ticket redemption arrives with a cookie. Use a high-entropy token (the default is) because the stored fingerprint is derived from it. Add a regression test: token A login, rebuild with token B, old cookie -> 401 on /ui/approvals and WS 4401. The DesktopControl part of this patch was validated in a scratch copy (rotation drops, same-token restart keeps, revoke_all, legacy-DB migration, repo session tests pass); the api.py route and web.py glue are sketches.

title: source_dir overlap guard compares path strings instead of filesystem identity: a second name for the data dir's project folder (bind mount; case variant on case-insensitive drvfs) bypasses it and copies the human token to the agent
description: SandboxManager.create (sandbox.py:397-405) resolves source_dir with Path.expanduser().resolve() and refuses it only if src == d, d in src.parents or src in d.parents for d in {settings.home.resolve(), db_path.resolve().parent}. resolve() only follows symlinks and keeps the caller's spelling, and Path equality and .parents membership are string decisions with no (st_dev, st_ino) or samefile check. Any second name for the data directory or one of its ancestors that is not a symlink therefore passes the guard. The accepted string becomes the read-only /source bind (sandbox.py:375, 415). The container's root setup 'cp -a /source/. /workspace/ && ... chown -R 1000:1000 /workspace' (sandbox.py:421-422, with CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE/CHOWN at 381) then copies the 0600 human_token (config.py:94-99) and agentbox.db into agent-owned /workspace. The agent can read them through read_file. That is the run-2 N-4 escalation from the lowest-trust principal (agent token, prompt-injected agent) to full human authority. Observed by the parent against the real Docker daemon with a dummy token, driving the same Service.create_sandbox and Service.call_tool that POST /sandboxes and POST /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/read_file call: a bind mount of the project dir (same inode, not a symlink) was ACCEPTED, and the agent's read_file of /workspace/data/human_token returned the real human token. The exact project path was REFUSED in the same run. v06 and p5r-v06 also showed with a fake Docker client that the string guard accepts case variants of the path, and p5r-v06 showed it still accepts a path that os.path.samefile reports identical to the project dir. On the case-sensitive test FS the case variant is a separate directory. A real case-insensitive alias (WSL2 /mnt/<drive> drvfs, which README.md:17 lists as supported, with ./data under the Windows-hosted project dir as the default per config.py:29) is the plausible natural trigger but was NOT observed. The trigger is operator-supplied (POST /sandboxes human_only, or a '*'-scope browser session via POST /ui/sandboxes). The CLI sends os.path.abspath(source), which keeps the shell's spelling. An agent cannot set source_dir. This is therefore a bypass of an operator-mistake safety control, not an attacker-chosen input. The compose deployment fails safe because its control plane sees only /var/lib/agentbox.
root_cause: The overlap check at sandbox.py:403-404 decides containment on resolved, spelling-preserving path strings (Path ==, .parents membership) instead of filesystem identity (os.path.samefile / st_dev+st_ino). Where two names resolve to one directory without being a symlink, such as a bind mount or a case variant on a case-insensitive filesystem, neither the data directory nor its ancestors are recognised, and the protected folder is mounted and copied to the agent.
intended_behavior: The comment at sandbox.py:401-402 states the intent: if the source folder overlaps the data folder, the human token, DB and other sandboxes' sources would be handed to the agent, so such a source_dir must be refused. The check should refuse every name for the data directory, its ancestors or its descendants, whatever the spelling or alias.

The accepted alias string becomes the read-only bind source at /source, so the daemon mounts the real data directory's parent.

Root 'cp -a /source/. /workspace/' plus chown -R 1000:1000 (line 422) with DAC_OVERRIDE (line 381) copies every file under /source, including the 0600 human_token and agentbox.db, into agent-owned /workspace, where the agent's read_file (sandbox.py:554-570, returned unchanged by api.py:205-211) returns them.

Refuse when src or any of its ancestors is os.path.samefile with a protected directory, or when a protected directory or any of its ancestors is samefile with src. It does not look inside src, so a mount of the data dir nested under src would still be copied by cp -a; refusing or skipping submounts during the copy (for example cp -ax, or checking that no path under src is samefile with a protected dir) would close that residual. Add a regression test with a bind mount or a case-insensitive fixture.

The parent's live run shows acceptance of an inode-identical alias and the agent reading the real token, with the exact path refused as a control; its code tree matches the audited tree. p5r-v06 independently confirmed the guard decision in sbx5. title: gui_strays exempts burst-launched uid-1001 processes from the stray kill based on window ownership, including the client-declared _NET_WM_PID
description: At GUI-burst close, AgentBox._stop_gui_strays collects uid-1001 processes and the set of window-owning pids and calls gui_strays. A new (non-baseline, non-exec-rooted) uid-1001 process that lives in a session that existed at burst start (base_sids) is spared whenever it is 'windowed': its own pid is in window_pids, or a NON-baseline ancestor's pid is in window_pids. window_pids come from `xdotool getwindowpid`, which returns the _NET_WM_PID property each X client sets for itself. Two routes can therefore spare background work started during the burst. (a) Without any forgery, a newly opened windowed app in the burst-start session (for example a file manager or editor started during the burst) exempts the scripts and children it spawns, because the ancestor clause only requires the windowed ancestor to be non-baseline. (b) A GUI client that declares another process's pid in _NET_WM_PID makes that process, even a headless one, look windowed. Either way the process can survive the close and keep modifying /workspace outside any monitored burst, which weakens the N-1 partial mitigation. Children of a PRE-EXISTING windowed baseline app are still killed, because the ancestor clause excludes baseline ancestors. Processes in a new session (terminal shells, setsid or nohup) are killed regardless of window (line 218). In the image, Xfce is started by the start script (agentbox-desktop-start:30), so apps launched from Xfce probably inherit a burst-start sid. This is not observable from source. The image has no python, xprop or compiler (Dockerfile:17-21), so route (b) needs a hand-written X client.
claimed_root_cause: Whether a new baseline-session process is spared is decided by window presence, derived from X window properties (including the client-settable _NET_WM_PID via xdotool getwindowpid) and a 'new windowed ancestor' heuristic, rather than by a control-plane-verifiable link such as the docker-exec ancestry already tracked. Target-controlled GUI clients, or any legitimately windowed app launched during the burst, therefore decide which of their descendants are treated as windowed apps or helpers and escape the kill.

trace.description: Burst close ingests attacker-influenced container output: calls desktop_processes(sid) to get the process list and window pids, then gui_strays to classify which new uid-1001 processes to kill.
Window pids come from `xdotool search --onlyvisible --name .` then `xdotool getwindowpid $w`, i.e. the client-set _NET_WM_PID property, parsed into the wins set at line 692.

A new baseline-session process is marked windowed (p.pid in window_pids, or a non-baseline ancestor pid in window_pids) and consequently NOT appended to the kill list at lines 223-224, so it survives the burst close.

evidence.description: wins = {int(x) ...} parsed from container-side xdotool getwindowpid output; the exemption input is controlled by the GUI clients inside the sandbox.

windowed = p.pid in window_pids or any(a.pid in window_pids and a.pid not in baseline for a in ancestors(p)); windowed -> not killed. The ancestor clause spares helpers of any newly created windowed app even with truthful window pids.

Docstring states windowed apps and their helpers (and burst-start processes and docker-exec-launched tools) are intentionally left running, so the only gate for a baseline-session process is window ownership.
startxfce4 is launched from the container start script, so Xfce-launched apps likely share a burst-start session id (base_sids) and are not caught by the new-session kill at sandbox.py:218.
_close_gui_burst pops the burst (233), runs the stray kill (235) and takes a single final manifest (236-240); nothing monitors /workspace afterwards, so any survivor's later writes are unrecorded.

blockers: Reachability in agentbox-desktop:0.1: whether, using only GUI input (click/type/key), a prompt-injected agent can get a uid-1001 process into a session that existed at burst start (base_sids) that either owns a visible window reported by `xdotool getwindowpid`, or descends from a newly created windowed process (for example a script run from a file manager or app window opened during the burst), or has its pid forged into another client's _NET_WM_PID. Real session ids (whether launcher, terminal or file-manager spawned processes inherit the Xfce start-script sid or get a new setsid session, which line 218 kills regardless) and real _NET_WM_PID values are not observable from source or from a pure-function harness over gui_strays, and the Docker daemon is unavailable offline. The pure-function harness already confirms the exemption logic itself.

validation_plan.local: In a disposable, network-less agentbox-desktop:0.1 sandbox: open a GUI burst with a GUI tool call. Using GUI input only, (a) open a file manager or editor window during the burst and from it run a script that appends a timestamp to a dummy file /workspace/_v15_probe every ~2s; and (b) separately, with a hand-written X client, set _NET_WM_PID of a window to the pid of a headless background writer started from a burst-start-session launcher. Just before close, record `ps -eo pid=,ppid=,sid=,uid=,args=` and `for w in $(xdotool search --onlyvisible --name .); do xdotool getwindowpid $w; done` to capture the real session ids and window-pid set, and feed them through the real gui_strays to predict survivors. Let the burst close on idle; then read the gui_processes_stopped audit entry and check whether /workspace/_v15_probe's mtime keeps advancing after close. Non-destructive: touches only the dummy probe file; kill the probe and discard the sandbox afterward.

Fix check: exempt only burst-start (baseline) processes and control-plane docker-exec-launched components, deriving ownership from a control-plane-verifiable link (for example the exec/ancestry already tracked) rather than window presence or the client-declared _NET_WM_PID. Non-destructive: dummy file only.

title: Prompt-injected agent writes unbounded, undeletable rows into the shared audit log via uncapped tool-call args
description: The agent token (lowest-trust principal, assumed prompt-injected) controls the free-form args dict of every tool call. service._call_tool writes an event=tool_request audit row with payload {"args": _logged_args(tool, args)} as its very first action, before policy.decide, so even denied or approval-requiring calls still persist the row. _logged_args only special-cases write_file content (replacing it with size+sha256); for every other tool and every other key the args pass through verbatim. No size cap exists at any layer: FastAPI/Starlette/uvicorn impose no default request-body limit, ToolCall.args is an unconstrained dict[str, Any], Settings has read/write/upload caps but no args/body cap, the shipped Caddy reverse_proxy has no request_body max_size, and audit.append serializes and INSERTs the payload with no size check. One request therefore persists an arbitrarily large row into the shared, append-only control-plane SQLite audit DB (a single DB for all sandboxes, on host disk). UPDATE/DELETE are blocked by triggers, so the operator cannot prune oversized rows without rebuilding the DB and destroying the hash chain. audit.verify() loads every row and rehashes each full payload, and /ui/verify calls audit.list(limit=100000), so one agent can permanently bloat the shared audit store and make the operator's own audit/verify tooling slow and memory-heavy for the life of the DB.
root_cause: _logged_args (service.py:131-137) returns agent args unchanged except write_file content, and _call_tool (service.py:297-298) persists them via audit.append before any policy decision; neither the HTTP layer (api.py:50-51,206-211), configuration (config.py:54-57), shipped proxy (deploy/Caddyfile:5) nor audit.append (audit.py:143-187) bounds the serialized payload; the append-only triggers (audit.py:35-38) make the oversized rows unrecoverable.
intended_behavior: Agent-supplied tool arguments recorded for audit are bounded in serialized size (as write_file content already is), so one lowest-trust request cannot persist an arbitrarily large, undeletable row into the shared audit DB or amplify the operator's verify/list path.

trace.description: Agent POSTs /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/{tool}; body.args is an unconstrained dict[str, Any] (api.py:50-51) passed straight to box.call_tool with actor=p.kind; no request-body or args size limit.

First action in the tool path: audit.append(event='tool_request', payload={'args': _logged_args(tool, args)}), executed before policy.decide (line 299), so the row persists even for calls that are later denied or sent to approval.

Static method returns the args dict unchanged for every tool except write_file; only write_file 'content' is replaced with content_bytes+content_sha256. All other keys/tools (e.g. a 3 MiB 'junk' value on read_file) pass through verbatim.
payload = self._mask(payload or {}); _mask recurses over the dict and json.dumps serializes it with no size check before the INSERT.
The full json.dumps(payload) is persisted into the append-only audit table; verify() (audit.py:208-233) and list(limit=100000) (web.py:270) later re-load and rehash every full row.

evidence.description: Only the write_file 'content' key is special-cased; every other tool/key is returned unchanged.
tool_request row appended as the first action, before policy.decide at line 299.
INSERT persists json.dumps(payload) with no size cap.
audit_no_update / audit_no_delete triggers (RAISE ABORT 'audit log is append-only') make oversized rows unprunable.
verify() selects all rows ORDER BY id and rehashes each full payload.
/ui/verify calls box.audit.list(sandbox_id=..., limit=100000), re-loading up to 100k full payloads.
Settings defines max_read_bytes/max_write_bytes/max_upload_bytes but no args/request-body cap.
Shipped behind-proxy deployment uses a bare 'reverse_proxy agentbox:8765' with no request_body max_size.
ToolCall.args: dict[str, Any] = {} is unconstrained; passed to box.call_tool (api.py:210) with no body limit.

conditions.description: Valid agent token for its own sandbox (lowest-trust network principal; threat model assumes a prompt-injected agent).
Each request appends one unprunable row sized to the body; recovery requires rebuilding the DB and losing the hash chain, since UPDATE/DELETE are trigger-blocked.
Both the default local serve and the shipped behind-proxy Caddy deployment lack a body cap; an operator-added body cap would reduce per-row magnitude but not cross-request accumulation.

execution.attacker_perspective: A prompt-injected agent adds a large junk field to tool args it already controls; the control plane records the full args into the shared append-only audit DB permanently and re-reads them on every operator verify/list.
payloads: POST /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/read_file  body {"args": {"path": "/workspace/x", "junk": "<3 MiB of 'A'>"}}
Repeat with list_dir, exec, key, type, etc. (any non-write_file tool, or any non-'content' key).
instructions: In the OS-enforced sandbox (sbx v08: /usr/bin/python3.13, /target read-only on sys.path, /scratch writable, no network, no Docker, uid 65534, 512 MiB, 1 CPU), reproduce service._logged_args verbatim and confirm a non-write_file args dict with a 3 MiB junk value is returned unchanged while write_file content is stripped.

Open agentbox.audit.AuditLog on a scratch DB and append actor='agent', event='tool_request', tool='read_file', payload={'args': logged_args(...)} with the 3 MiB junk; measure length(payload) of the stored row.
Append 3 more rows with junk; sum length(payload).
Attempt DELETE and UPDATE on a row; observe the append-only triggers.
Call verify() and list(limit=100000).
execution.observed_result: logged_args kept the 3,145,728-byte junk key unchanged (write_file content was stripped); the stored row's payload was 3,145,774 bytes; 4 rows totalled 12,583,024 bytes; both DELETE and UPDATE raised sqlite3.IntegrityError 'audit log is append-only'; verify() returned ok=True after re-checking all 4 rows; list(limit=100000) returned all 4 rows with the full 3 MiB payload intact. Independently reproduced in sbx v08 (/scratch DB); see agents/v08/artifacts/repro_v08.out (consistent with the hunter's agents/h-buffer/artifacts/audit_cap.out).

remediation.strategy: Bound the serialized size of the agent-supplied args that reach the audit log, after the existing write_file content strip and for every tool, so the cap cannot be sidestepped by combining write_file content with an extra large key. When the json-serialized args exceed a fixed limit, store a byte count, sha256 and a truncated head. Keep content_bytes and content_sha256 in the truncated form, since the approval preview uses them. The same _logged_args also feeds the approval payload (service.py:167 and :408), so the fix covers those rows too. Add a request-body/args size limit on the tool endpoint (and a request_body max_size in the shipped Caddyfile) as defense in depth.

likelihood.reason: The agent controls the args dict in normal operation; adding a large field is trivial with its own token and requires no special conditions.

impact.reason: Persistent, unprunable growth of the shared append-only audit DB (single DB for all sandboxes, on host disk) plus memory/CPU amplification on every operator verify()/ui-verify list(100000); recovery requires rebuilding the DB and losing the hash chain. Not RCE or a guaranteed crash.

confidence.reason: Every layer read from source: uncapped pass-through in _logged_args, pre-decision persistence, absence of any HTTP/config/proxy/audit body or row cap, append-only triggers, and full re-read in verify/list all confirmed. Uncapped persistence, trigger-blocked DELETE/UPDATE, and full re-read independently reproduced in the sandbox (repro_v08.out).

title: GUI burst open treats failed container-side collection as success (empty baseline or no burst) with no audit record
description: When the first agent GUI input of a burst arrives, AgentBox._snapshot takes a docker-commit snapshot and then calls _open_gui_burst. That method collects the /workspace manifest and the desktop process baseline. Two silent fail-open paths exist. (a) Exit status unchecked (observed live): SandboxManager.workspace_manifest runs the root `find ... | head -c` exec and returns `_parse_manifest(res.output[0] or b"")` without checking res.exit_code. If the in-container command cannot run, it returns ({}, False) with no exception, and _open_gui_burst records the burst against an empty baseline. desktop_processes and kill_processes ignore exec status in the same way. At close, the diff reports every pre-existing file as added. The audit event carries counts and truncated=True plus only the first 100 sorted paths, so the real GUI-made change can fall outside the listed paths, and nothing records that the baseline collection failed. Parent-live l7 measured this on agentbox-desktop:0.1 with the pids cgroup at 1022-1024/1024, using pressure created by direct docker exec as uid 1001: the manifest had 0 entries, the burst was recorded, the audit showed only tool_request/policy_decision/snapshot/tool_result, and a close after the pressure ended gave gui_changes added=301, truncated=True, with the real change zz_changed_by_gui.txt absent from the listed 100. (b) Exception swallowed: if either collector raises, the bare `except Exception: return` at service.py:210 records no burst. Later GUI inputs inside the idle/interval window open no new burst, so there is no stray kill and no gui_changes for that window. The same pattern at :221 and :238 skips the kill or the diff at close. A mock reproduces this, but no agent-reachable raising trigger is known. Agent reachability (parent-live l9): an approval-free exec under the default read-only-exec rule (uid 1000) filled the pids cgroup to 1024/1024 within about 1 s, and a concurrent agent GUI input (key shift) still returned 200 and recorded a burst with 0 manifest entries and no audit marker. The pressure did not release itself: the exec ended with exit 254, about 1000 uid-1000 processes survived, pids stayed at 1022/1024 even after a root `pkill -x tail` by the parent, and a close under that pressure logged no gui_changes at all. A sandbox wedged this way can start no new processes, which limits what the agent can do while the condition holds. Not yet shown: an agent-only sequence that ends with a misleading or absent gui_changes record while a real GUI-made change exists. Bounds: the burst snapshot is still taken and logged, so the restore point survives. gui_changes is a detective, partial control, and the GUI is approval-free by design (N-1). Provenance: the l7/l9 scripts imported the working branch /home/user/agentbox rather than the audited tree. The burst, collector and policy code they exercise is byte-identical between the two, so the results apply to the audited source. The decisive live runs are the parent's.
claimed_root_cause: Burst bookkeeping treats a failed container-side collection as a successful one. workspace_manifest (sandbox.py:495-501), desktop_processes (sandbox.py:689-692) and kill_processes (sandbox.py:697) never check exec exit status, and _open_gui_burst/_stop_gui_strays/_close_gui_burst (service.py:210, 221, 238) swallow every exception. In both cases there is no audit event and no fail-closed fallback, such as refusing further GUI input or marking the burst baseline invalid.

trace.description: Agent token (lowest-trust principal, own sandbox) sends a GUI input tool (key/click/type). Policy default is allow, with no approval.
On an allowed GUI input that starts a burst (_gui_needs_snapshot true), it calls _snapshot.
After docker commit, it opens the GUI burst with the new snapshot id.

title: Human screen takeover (safety override) blocks behind an untimed agent GUI exec holding gui_lock while the in-container X server is unresponsive
description: Agent GUI tools (screenshot/click/type/key) run through AgentBox._run_tool, which acquires desktop.gui_lock(sid) and calls SandboxManager._x -> docker exec_run (scrot/xdotool) with no container-side timeout wrapper, unlike exec (timeout -k 5), read_file and outbox_read (timeout -k 2 30). takeover and handback acquire the same plain threading.Lock via `with`, with no acquisition deadline. If the X server stops answering while an agent GUI exec is outstanding, that exec blocks inside the held lock, so the human takeover (the safety override for a misbehaving screen) and handback queue behind it. Source chain verified at the cited lines; gui_lock is a plain threading.Lock (desktop.py:155-158). Parent-live evidence (the parent's, not the verifier's; no Docker here): l1_takeover.py SIGSTOPs Xvfb (uid desktop=1001) in a real desktop sandbox, issues an agent screenshot that hangs holding gui_lock, then starts a takeover: it does not return within 20 s. l10_bound.py (after Phase 3) ran the same setup for 150 s: after 151 s both the screenshot and the takeover were still blocked, and both returned only after SIGCONT (screenshot 153 s, takeover 151 s). So the hang is not capped by the docker SDK client timeout and the lock is not released by a ReadTimeout, which settles the bound: the lockout lasts as long as X stays unresponsive. Not yet established: that a prompt-injected agent, using only its own agent-token capabilities, can itself make X unresponsive. The parent's SIGSTOP was a docker exec as uid 1001, standing in for a GUI terminal step (N-1). Source makes it plausible: the type/key tools can drive xfce4-terminal (Dockerfile:19), which runs as the same uid as Xvfb, and a process may signal another process of its own uid.
claimed_root_cause: gui_lock is held across SandboxManager._x exec_run with no container-side timeout wrapper (unlike exec/read_file/outbox_read, which use `timeout -k`), and takeover/handback acquire the same plain threading.Lock unconditionally with no acquisition deadline, so a hung GUI exec serializes the human safety override behind it for as long as the in-container X server is unresponsive.

Runs c.exec_run(argv, user=desktop, ...) for scrot/xdotool with no container-side `timeout -k` wrapper, so the exec blocks for as long as X is unresponsive.
Human takeover (safety override) acquires the same gui_lock via a plain `with` (no deadline) and cannot return until the hung GUI exec releases it.

By contrast, exec wraps argv in a container-side `timeout -k 5 <t>`; read_file (561) and outbox_read (665) use `timeout -k 2 30`; _x has no equivalent bound.

title: Idle GUI burst close runs another sandbox's untimed docker execs inline on unrelated tool threads and human approval/audit threads
description: close_idle_gui_bursts() iterates every sandbox's open GUI burst and is called before the per-sandbox tool_concurrency check at the start of every call_tool (service.py:273), from expire_stale (service.py:373, reached by GET /approvals, GET /approvals/{aid}, and POST /approvals/{aid} via decide->expire_stale at 385), and from GET /audit (api.py:258). Closing sandbox B's burst runs desktop_processes (ps + an xdotool search via _x) and workspace_manifest (find) and kill_processes against B's container with docker exec_run and no deadline. So B's maintenance runs on sandbox A's tool_pool thread or on a human request (Starlette threadpool) thread, outside B's tool_concurrency budget. If B's container/X server is unresponsive, the exec never returns and the unrelated caller blocks indefinitely. The burst is popped before closing (service.py:232), so one idle stuck burst permanently steals one caller thread; aggregating across many desktop sandboxes can exhaust the shared pools. The parent reproduced the cross-sandbox block against the real Docker-backed control plane: with B's Xvfb stopped and B's burst idle, A's list_dir did not return within 20s and returned 0.3s after B's Xvfb resumed.
root_cause: close_idle_gui_bursts() runs cross-sandbox maintenance (burst close) inline on whatever thread calls it - a tool_pool thread of an unrelated sandbox (service.py:273, before the tool_concurrency check at 275-278) or a human request thread (expire_stale service.py:373 from GET/POST approvals and decide; GET /audit api.py:258) - and the docker execs it performs (desktop_processes xdotool via _x sandbox.py:684/690-691, workspace_manifest find 499, kill_processes 697) use exec_run with no deadline, unlike exec/read_file/outbox_read which wrap the command in 'timeout'. An unresponsive owning container therefore blocks the unrelated caller indefinitely, with the work charged to no sandbox's budget.
intended_behavior: Work done for sandbox B should be charged to B's tool_concurrency budget and never run inline on another sandbox's tool thread or a human request thread, and every docker exec (as exec/read_file/outbox_read already do) should carry a deadline so an unresponsive container cannot stall unrelated sandboxes or the human approval/audit path.

Pops burst B (232) then calls _stop_gui_strays(B) (235) before workspace_manifest (237).
Calls self.sandboxes.desktop_processes(B) (218) against sandbox B's container.

The calling thread (sandbox A's tool_pool thread or a human request thread) blocks in exec_start until B's X server replies; a stopped/unresponsive Xvfb never replies and exec_run has no deadline. workspace_manifest find (499) and kill_processes (697) on the same path are likewise untimed.

The defect also triggers on benign causes (a slow or overloaded desktop container, a slow Docker exec), so exposure is not solely attacker-gated.

title: GUI burst stray-kill and gui_changes logging are lost across sandbox restore and pause
description: GUI input bypasses the approval gate by design (N-1). The partial mitigation for that is a per-burst snapshot, a gui_changes audit record and killing the uid-1001 processes started during the burst (service.py:206-256). None of the GUI burst state (_gui_burst, _gui_input_at, _gui_snap_at) is reconciled with container lifecycle transitions. (1) Restore: api.py:192 and web.py:243 call end_desktop, which closes the old burst (service.py:531). It clears _gui_input_at only through handback when a human lease exists (service.py:494), and it never clears _gui_snap_at. After the restore, an agent GUI input that comes within gui_snapshot_idle (60 s) of its previous input and within gui_snapshot_interval (600 s) of the last GUI snapshot gets False from _gui_needs_snapshot (service.py:196). It therefore runs with no snapshot and no burst. A uid-1001 background process the agent starts in that gap is recorded in the next burst's baseline pid set (service.py:213), so gui_strays skips it (sandbox.py:216) and it is never killed. Workspace changes made in the gap are in the next burst's baseline manifest, so they never appear in gui_changes. (2) Pause: the pause route (api.py:166-170) does no burst handling. Once the burst's idle time passes while the sandbox is paused, the next caller of close_idle_gui_bursts closes it: the sandbox page polls /ui/audit every 3 s (templates/sandbox.html:19, web.py:261), and GET /audit, expire_stale and any call_tool also call it. _close_gui_burst pops the burst first (service.py:232). desktop_processes then raises through _desktop/_require_running for a paused sandbox (sandbox.py:688, 468-469) and the error is swallowed (service.py:221-222). The manifest exec against the paused container also fails and is swallowed (238-239). The strays are not killed and the changes are not logged. After resume they keep running and become part of the next burst's baseline. The same unreconciled state also causes an availability effect, reproduced only in the fake harness. Restore pops the burst in end_desktop before the container is replaced, and nothing invalidates a burst opened after that point. If an agent GUI input opens a burst between end_desktop and the container swap (a race window), the baseline holds the old container's pids. When that burst idles out, gui_strays treats every uid-1001 process of the new desktop session as a stray and kills it. Windowed processes are included, because base_sids is empty when the old pids are absent from the new container. This happens only when the new container's pids differ from the old ones. With identical pids nothing is killed.
root_cause: GUI burst bookkeeping in AgentBox is in-memory state keyed only by sandbox id. It has no tie to the container instance or its run state. end_desktop (service.py:529-537), which the restore routes call, closes the burst but leaves _gui_input_at (cleared only by handback at 494) and _gui_snap_at (set at 263, never cleared) in place. _gui_needs_snapshot (195-197) therefore suppresses a fresh burst after restore, and a burst opened after end_desktop survives the container swap. The pause and resume routes (api.py:166-176) do not touch burst state at all. _close_gui_burst (232) also discards the burst before its enforcement steps, and those steps return silently on failure (221-222, 238-239). An idle close while the sandbox is paused therefore drops the burst without killing strays or logging changes.
intended_behavior: Every container lifecycle change (restore, pause, resume, delete) resets the GUI burst timers, so the first GUI input afterwards takes a snapshot and opens a burst whose baseline belongs to the current container. A burst is discarded only after its strays have been stopped and its changes diffed and logged. A paused sandbox keeps its burst until it is running again, or the burst is closed before pausing. A burst whose container id no longer matches is closed without killing anything.

instructions: In the sbx sandbox (no network, no Docker), run /usr/bin/python3.13 -I /scratch/v12_burst.py. It builds the real AgentBox with a real AuditLog, ApprovalStore, Policy.load(default_policy.yaml) and DesktopControl, and the real gui_strays. Only SandboxManager is faked: it records snapshots and kills; desktop_processes and click raise when paused, mirroring _require_running; workspace_manifest raises when paused, mirroring Docker refusing exec in a paused container. time.monotonic is patched to drive the timers.

Drive the agent through box.call_tool(sid, 'click', ...) and the human restore through box.end_desktop followed by the fake restore, as api.py:192-193 does. Pause and resume flip the record status, as api.py:169/175 do. Call close_idle_gui_bursts as the UI poll does. execution.observed_result: Control: snapshot snap_1, stray 50 killed, gui_processes_stopped [50] and gui_changes modified [report.md] logged. Restore: after end_desktop the burst is closed but _gui_input_at and _gui_snap_at are kept. The t20 and t70 inputs return 200 with no snapshot and no burst. The next burst (t200, snap_2) has baseline [1,10,11,12,60]. Killed []. Stray 60 still alive. No gui_processes_stopped or gui_changes event. With the timers cleared after restore (proposed fix), t20 opens snap_2, stray 60 is killed and report.md is logged. Pause: the idle close while paused drops the burst. Killed []. Stray 70 is alive after resume. Next baseline [1,10,11,12,70]; stray 70 is still alive after the next idle close; no gui_* events. Stale baseline: a burst opened after end_desktop on the old container, with baseline [1,10,11,12], kills every uid-1001 process of the new container [14,15,16], including the windowed panel.
